name: OpenSSH ssh client
summary: The OpenSSH ssh client implementing layered SSH transport, user authentication, and connection-channel control for remote sessions, forwarding, and multiplexed data streams.

features.name: Layered SSH session establishment
features.description: OpenSSH's ssh client drives transport connection and key exchange, user authentication, and the ssh-connection service as separate protocol phases. The official OpenSSH overview describes transport confidentiality/integrity, authentication mechanisms, and connection-layer services as distinct layers.
benefits: Separates cryptographic transport, identity proof, and channel services
Permits authentication mechanisms and channel services to evolve within protocol boundaries
costs: Phase ordering and negotiated algorithms create compatibility state
Security properties depend on correct host and user authentication policy

features.name: Multiplexed flow-controlled channels
features.description: The SSH connection protocol multiplexes sessions, forwarded TCP connections, and other services into channels over one encrypted connection. OpenSSH maintains channel objects, per-channel file descriptors, windows, packet sizes, callbacks, and lifecycle state.
benefits: Shares one authenticated transport across several logical services
Provides per-channel flow control and independent close semantics
costs: Channel windows and shared transport scheduling add coordination state
A single connection failure can affect multiple logical channels

features.name: Session, command, and forwarding services
features.description: ssh can request a shell, remote command, subsystem, pseudo-terminal, X11 forwarding, or TCP forwarding through connection-layer channel and global requests. These are distinct service requests carried by the same channel framework.
benefits: Unifies interactive login, command execution, and forwarding under one transport
Allows service-specific requests without separate network connections
costs: Forwarding and agent/X11 capabilities expand authority beyond command execution
Service success and remote process exit are reported asynchronously through channel messages

mathematical_views.question: How does a client advance from transport setup through key exchange, authentication, service request, and channel operation?
assumptions: Protocol phases have explicit success and failure transitions
Negotiation and authentication results control later channel availability
The view abstracts cryptographic primitive internals

mathematical_views.question: How do logical SSH channels share one connection while respecting per-channel windows and close state?
assumptions: The encrypted connection is a shared transport vertex
Channels are independently identified state vertices with window and packet constraints
The view abstracts kernel sockets and event-loop scheduling

mathematical_views.question: Which authenticated peers and channel requests can create sessions or forwarded TCP connections under client configuration?
assumptions: Authentication establishes the principal before service requests
Forwarding permissions are policy inputs rather than inherent protocol guarantees
The relation does not infer authorization from mere channel syntax

benefits: Clear separation of transport security, identity, and services
costs: Negotiation and phase failure handling increase protocol complexity

benefits: Several logical services share one authenticated connection
costs: Per-channel flow control and shared failure boundaries require coordination

benefits: One client supports terminal, command, subsystem, and forwarding use cases
costs: Optional forwarding services increase authority and attack-surface assumptions
